An Introduction to Species: So far, the focus has been microevolution, which is a change in the frequencies of genotypes in a population. This chapter moves up a level, to macroevolution: how new species form, how fast that happens, and how species are lost.
The Definition of a Species: A species is defined as a group

Start with what a species is. Under the biological species concept, which comes from Ernst Mayr, a species is a group of natural populations that actually or potentially interbreed, and that are reproductively isolated from other such groups. In other words, members can produce viable, fertile offspring with each other, but not with outsiders.

That is not the only definition. The morphological species concept defines a species by body shape, size, and other structural features. The lineage species concept defines it as organisms that share a branch on the tree of life, usually judged from DNA.

Looks can mislead, though. Two meadowlarks can appear virtually identical and still be different species, because they are reproductively isolated. And humans can look very different from one another while being one species.
The definition does not apply to asexual organisms
The definition cannot be applied to fossils

The biological definition has its own problems. It does not apply to organisms that reproduce asexually, such as many microbes. And it cannot be applied to fossils, which show structure but not who could breed with whom. That is why fossil species are identified by the morphological concept.
The definition encompasses animals that actually or potentially interbreed

The third problem is the phrase potentially interbreed, which is not well defined. Polar bears and grizzly bears are the classic case. Their ranges are starting to overlap, hybrids have been found in the wild, and those hybrids are fertile. Strictly speaking, the definition would make them one species, yet they are still classified as two.
Reproductive Barriers: Reproductive barriers between species can come in two forms
What keeps species apart are reproductive barriers, and they come in two forms. Prezygotic barriers prevent a zygote from forming at all. Postzygotic barriers act after a zygote has formed.

There are five prezygotic barriers. Habitat isolation means two groups are separated by space and never meet. Temporal isolation means they are separated by time. For example, the wood frog's mating peaks at the end of March and the leopard frog's at the beginning of April, and a difference of a few weeks is enough.

Behavioral isolation depends on mating signals. Two species of crabs on the South Carolina coast look almost identical, but one waves its large claw in a figure-eight and the other waves it differently, so the wrong signal attracts no mate.

Mechanical isolation means the parts simply do not fit, as with two sage plants whose petals suit pollinating insects of different sizes. And gametic isolation means that sperm and egg will not fuse, even when they meet.
these different kinds of prezygotic barriers are not exclusive
These barriers often work together. In the frogs, timing alone does not fully separate the two populations. Species-specific mating calls, which is behavioral isolation, do the rest.

Postzygotic barriers come down to reproductive success. With reduced hybrid survivorship, the offspring are not viable and die soon after birth. With reduced hybrid fertility, the offspring live but cannot reproduce. The mule, from a male donkey and a female horse, is the standard example: it lives a full life, but it is sterile.
The establishment of a barrier to gene flow allows

Once a barrier cuts off gene flow, the separated populations drift apart through mutation. Usually that ends the possibility of interbreeding, but not always. European and American sycamores can still interbreed after more than 20 million years apart, which is why Mayr's definition says actually or potentially.
The Formation of New Species: New species form in two broad ways: allopatric speciation and sympatric speciation. Expect both on the exam.
Allopatric Speciation: Allopatric speciation occurs when a geographic barrier

Allopatric speciation happens when a geographic barrier divides a population, or when part of a population crosses a barrier and founds a new one. The word means other country, and it is the most common form of speciation, especially in animals.
one kind of plant exists in mountains

Picture a plant growing on the mountains on both sides of a valley. The valley floods, gene flow between the two sides stops, and each population changes on its own. How fast depends on factors such as body size, temperature, and UV exposure.

Two real examples. Drosophila fruit flies began on a single Hawaiian island and spread to the others, and even the wet and dry sides of one island were enough to separate them. Today roughly 25 percent of all Drosophila species live in Hawaii, helped along by their short generation times.

Antelope squirrels in the desert Southwest live on opposite sides of a canyon. The two species look almost the same, but they have diverged so far genetically that they could not reproduce even if they were put back together.
The Dobzhansky-Muller model is a simple model

How does one lineage become two? The Dobzhansky-Muller model explains it. A population is split into two isolated groups. Over time, each group fixes a different beneficial mutation, at a different place in the genome. When the two groups meet again, those mutant alleles are incompatible with each other, so the groups can no longer interbreed.
also applies to major chromosomal rearrangements

The same model covers whole chromosome changes. In Rhogeessa bats, chromosomes fused at the centromere in different patterns in different groups, so the chromosomes could not line up during meiosis. This route is less common, and these bats are the best-known case.
Reproductive isolation tends to increase as species diverge

In general, reproductive isolation increases as two groups diverge genetically. But the graph of species pairs shows an important exception: a small amount of divergence in certain key genes can produce high reproductive isolation, sometimes within a single generation.
Sympatric Speciation: Sympatric speciation occurs when species arise
Sympatric speciation happens when a new species arises inside a population that stays connected. There is no physical barrier, yet gene flow is still cut off. The word means same country.
For a long time, evolutionary biologists argued

It is more common in plants than in animals, although recent research shows it happens in animals more often than scientists once believed. It is hard to prove, because you have to show the populations diverged with no barrier between them.
Sympatric speciation by polyploidy

There are two causes. The first is polyploidy, mostly in plants. A mistake in cell division produces an individual with extra copies of the genome. It can live, and often fertilize itself, but it cannot reproduce with the normal diploid individuals around it. So a new species can form essentially instantly, and this is thought to be the main way plants speciate.
Autopolyploidy exists
Allopolyploidy exists
It comes in two forms. In autopolyploidy, the extra chromosome sets all come from the same species. In allopolyploidy, they come from different species.
Why are tetraploids reproductively isolated

Why is a tetraploid cut off from diploids? A diploid makes haploid gametes and a tetraploid makes diploid gametes. Together they produce a triploid, with three copies of each chromosome, and most of its gametes are unbalanced. The triploid is an evolutionary dead end.
a tetraploid species of tree frog
Polyploidy is rare in animals overall

Polyploidy is rare in animals, but amphibians are the major exception, especially salamanders and newts. One example is Hyla versicolor, a tetraploid tree frog in the southeastern United States, which can no longer reproduce with its diploid ancestors.
Sympatric speciation by behavioral change
The second cause is a change in behavior, which is how it happens in animals. The individuals could still meet, but some difference in behavior keeps them apart, and eventually gene flow stops.
These flies originally laid their eggs

Apple maggot flies originally laid their eggs on hawthorn fruit. When apples were introduced, some flies came to prefer them, and a fly tends to eat the fruit it was born on. Hawthorns and apple trees can grow side by side, yet that one preference has split the flies into two groups.
sockeye salmon are anadromous

Sockeye salmon return to the exact creek where they were born, and they find it by smell. Art Hasler showed this by plugging their nasal passages with cotton, which left the fish completely disoriented. So when a few salmon swim up the wrong creek and breed there, their descendants keep returning to it. The six species of Pacific salmon are thought to have arisen that way.
Cichlids are colorful fish

And some African lakes hold several hundred species of cichlid fishes in a single lake. They divided up by behavior, some eating snails and others something else, and some using different parts of the lake.
reproductive isolation is involved in both sympatric speciation and allopatric
Notice what the two kinds of speciation share. In both, a barrier to gene flow leads to genetic differentiation, and that leads to reproductive isolation.
Adaptive Radiation: Adaptive radiation is a burst of speciation: many new and diverse species evolving relatively quickly from one common ancestor, usually after exposure to new environments. Darwin's finches are the classic case, with 13 or 14 species on the Galapagos Islands from a single ancestor. Keep in mind that quickly, in evolutionary time, can still mean millions of years.
The evolution of cichlid fishes in African lakes
The evolution of Drosophila fruit flies
The evolution of Hawaiian silversword plants
Other examples are the cichlid fishes of the African lakes, the Drosophila fruit flies of Hawaii, and the Hawaiian silversword plants, which now number about 35 species.
Coevolution: Coevolution refers to the evolutionary influence

Species do not evolve alone. Coevolution is the influence two interacting species have on each other's evolution. The acacia tree in Africa houses acacia ants in its swollen thorns and feeds them a sugary secretion. In return, the ants swarm any herbivore that tries to eat the tree, even an elephant.
definitely need to know the Red Queen hypothesis

That leads to the Red Queen hypothesis, which you need to know for the exam. Because species are coevolving, each one has to keep evolving just to survive. When one changes, the other must change to keep up. Neither gains an advantage over the other. Both are running just to stay in the same place.

One open question to keep in mind is the latitudinal gradient of biodiversity. Species richness is highest in the tropics and declines toward the poles, and no hypothesis fully explains why. Biodiversity at any moment is a balance between two rates, speciation and extinction, and those come next.
The Tempo of Speciation: we will be considering the rate of evolution and extinction
So what controls how fast evolution proceeds, and how quickly new species form?
Two Paradigms for the Tempo of Speciatio: There are two models. Gradualism says that DNA mutates slowly and steadily, so isolated populations diverge little by little over millions of years. Punctuated equilibrium says that species sit in long periods of stasis, interrupted by sudden episodes of speciation. That model was proposed around 1972 by Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould.

Which one is right? Both. The fossil record shows slow change punctuated by rapid change, although most biologists today would probably say punctuated equilibrium describes speciation better in general.

Cichlids are the example of punctuated equilibrium. In Lake Victoria, 400 species evolved in just 12,000 years, which is almost instant in evolutionary time. Much of it came from groups specializing on different diets within the same lake.
Horseshoe crabs are the example of gradualism. Their form has stayed essentially the same for 100 million years, even though the environment changed enormously.

Two more terms. In anagenesis, one lineage changes gradually until it counts as a new species, so the number of species stays the same. In cladogenesis, a new species branches off while the ancestor persists, so biodiversity increases by one.
What Controls the Rate of Speciation?: Three things set the rate of speciation. The first is the rate of mutation, the ultimate source of genetic diversity. The second is the rate of selection, which depends on competition for food, mates, and space, and on generation time. Bacteria, with short generations, should evolve faster than desert tortoises. The third is the rate of environmental change, which intensifies natural selection.
mutation rates in ectotherms increase exponentially

Temperature matters too. Dr. Gillooly's research finds that mutation rates in ectotherms rise exponentially with temperature, because warmth speeds up cell division. All else equal, an organism living at 20 degrees Celsius has a mutation rate roughly 300 percent higher than one living at 10 degrees.
Which of these factors matters most

Which factor matters most? It depends, and biologists cannot yet predict speciation rates for a particular species. As a rule of thumb, short generation times and rapid environmental change both make speciation more likely.
Exaptation: natural selection must start with structures
Natural selection can only work with structures that already exist. An exaptation is a structure that evolved for one purpose and came to be used for another.

Wings are one example. Early birds such as Archaeopteryx already had feathered limbs, probably used to run up trees and gain lift, and those were modified step by step into wings for powered flight. Moray eels are another. Their extra set of jaws, which pulls prey down the throat, came from modified gill arches.
Causes of Rapid Speciation: What makes speciation happen fast? One cause is a key genetic change such as polyploidy, where the genome doubles or triples and the new organism can no longer mate with the rest. That is especially common in plants.

Another is a change in the genes that control development. Hox genes organize the body plan early on, so even a small mutation can have a dramatic effect. In flies, a single Hox mutation can make legs grow where the antennae should be.
A third is heterochrony, which is a change in the timing or the order of developmental events.
Allometric heterochrony is a change in the rate of growth or development. Most domesticated dogs reach maturity, and their full size, earlier than wolves do, which is why adult dogs are smaller.
hinted that neoteny would definitely be on the exam

Sequence heterochrony is a change in when a structure appears. The axolotl, a large Mexican salamander, keeps its gills into adulthood. Adults retaining juvenile traits is called neoteny, and you should expect it on the exam.
The theory is that humans have retained
Some scientists think humans show neoteny as well, because our flat faces resemble a juvenile chimpanzee's skull more than an adult's. The idea has been proposed, but it is hard to confirm.
The Tempo of Extinction: extinction removes species from the Earth
Speciation adds species, and extinction removes them. Like speciation, extinction runs at a steady background rate, speeds up with environmental change, and sometimes comes in bursts.
current extinction rate is higher than ever
in the last 250 years

Right now it is far from background. The current extinction rate is about 100 to 1,000 times higher than the rate seen in the fossil record, and it could reach about 10,000 times. The cause is us: habitat loss, development, pollution, climate change, and population growth. That is why the present age is called the anthropocene.
Extinction threatens some organisms more than others

Some groups are hit harder. About 43 percent of amphibian species are threatened, mainly by the chytrid fungus, a skin infection that has spread worldwide and cannot yet be controlled. Insects are declining too. A 2018 study found a 76 percent drop in insect biomass in Germany over about 30 years, and almost no one had noticed.
Rapid bursts of extinction
important to know the Cretaceous and Permian
A mass extinction is a rapid burst in which more than 50 percent of species are lost. There have been five, and many believe we are now in the sixth. Know two of them for the exam.
The Cretaceous mass extinction, which wiped out
there is a consensus about the Cretaceous

The Cretaceous mass extinction, 65 million years ago, wiped out about 71 percent of all species, including the non-avian dinosaurs. It is thought to have been triggered by a meteor impact in the Yucatan Peninsula, which left a crater 112 miles wide. Dust blocked the sunlight, plants and plankton died, and the animals that ate them followed.
The Permian mass extinction wiped out
still uncertain about what caused the Permian

The Permian mass extinction, 250 million years ago, was worse. It wiped out about 83 percent of all genera, and 97 percent of aquatic genera. Its cause is still uncertain. One idea is massive volcanic eruptions and a release of methane. Among the few survivors was Lystrosaurus, a pig-sized herbivore thought to be an ancestor of modern mammals.
periods of mass extinction are almost always followed
Mass extinctions are almost always followed by bursts of speciation, because the survivors meet new opportunities. The age of mammals followed the Cretaceous extinction.
as a snapshot of the interaction between speciation and extinction
This version plots 3,000 species

Finally, think of the tree of life as a snapshot of speciation and extinction working together. The usual branching diagrams tempt people to think some species are more evolved than others. A circular tree built from the ribosomal RNA of 3,000 species makes the point better: all living things are related, and none sits above the rest.
